html:
A Buddhist temple in Nara, once one of its Seven Great Temples and today, like Kōfuku-ji, a head temple of the Hossō school. Emperor Tenmu ordered it in 680 as an offering for the recovery of his consort, who later reigned as Empress Jitō. He died before it was done, and she finished it in Fujiwara-kyō, the capital of the time, around 698. It is named for its main image, Yakushi, the Medicine Buddha.

After the court moved to Heijō-kyō, now Nara, in 710, the temple was moved there; the move has long been dated to 718, though digs at the old site in the 1990s suggest the two temples may have stood at the same time. Its plan, called the Yakushi-ji style, puts the Golden Hall in the middle with two pagodas set symmetrically east and west in front of it. The East Pagoda, finished in 730, is the only building left from the eighth century. It is 34 m high and has three storeys, but small roofs between them make it look like six, and a distinctive finial tops it. The Golden Hall holds the Yakushi triad, the Medicine Buddha between two attendants, an early Japanese work in the Tang Chinese style; scholars still argue whether it was made for the first temple or the second.

Fires destroyed most of the temple in 973 and the Golden Hall in 1528. The Golden Hall was rebuilt in 1976, the West Pagoda in 1981 and the central gate in 1984. The East Pagoda was taken apart for repair from 1898 to 1900 and again from 2012, when its central pillar had rotted and its eaves sagged. The temple is part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
